structure.title: First impressions
structure.text: Visits and assemblies establish attractions, rivalries, and judgments before anyone knows much about the others.

structure.title: Reconsideration
structure.text: Journeys, letters, and changed circumstances put those judgments under pressure and reveal their practical consequences.

people.name: Elizabeth Bennet
people.text: The second of five Bennet daughters, quick, witty and fond of a laugh, who trusts her first impressions of people and enjoys being right.

people.name: Darcy
people.text: A rich gentleman from Derbyshire who arrives in the neighbourhood with his friend Bingley and is thought proud and disagreeable from his first ball.

people.name: Jane Bennet
people.text: The eldest and most beautiful Bennet sister, gentle and slow to think ill of anyone, who is drawn to Mr Bingley from their first meeting.

context.title: Inheritance and marriage
context.text: The Bennet estate will pass away from the daughters. Marriage therefore concerns future housing and income as well as affection.

passages.quote: a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.

context.title: Narrative irony
context.text: The narration can borrow a character's assumptions while allowing readers to notice their limits. A confident sentence need not be a final verdict.

notice.why: Flattering information can feel more credible than unwelcome facts.
Polite forms carry decisions about rank and belonging.

opening: Elizabeth Bennet hears a wealthy stranger dismiss her as not attractive enough to dance with, and finds him easy to dislike. His manners do little to change her mind. In a family where marriage can determine a woman’s future security, she takes particular pleasure in refusing to be impressed by his fortune. Austen gives Elizabeth the wit to expose other people’s absurdities, then puts her judgment to a harder test: recognising how readily she believes a story that flatters her opinion of herself.
